title: Stand-Up Pt II
summary: Part two of a two-part Stuff You Should Know episode on stand-up comedy. The hosts discuss early 1990s alt comedy (venues like Largo, Luna Lounge, Big and Tall Books; Mr. Show; Mitch Hedberg), the influence of podcasts and social media on booking, one-person shows and "claptor" comedy (Hannah Gadsby's Nanette, Tig Notaro, Mulaney, John Hodgman), crowd work (Big Jay Oakerson, Rory Scoville), the psychology and health of comedians (OLIFE traits, shorter lifespans per a 2016 Australian study), how to start doing stand-up (writing five minutes, open mics, joke structure), whether any topics should be off limits (Sarah Silverman, Ronny Chang, Dave Chappelle), the rise of right-leaning podcast comics, and listener mail about the novel Paper Ghosts.
topics: Stuff You Should Know part two

segments.title: Opening
segments.summary: Josh introduces part two of the stand-up comedy episode.

segments.title: Alt comedy origins
segments.summary: Chuck explains alt comedy emerging in the early 1990s, performed in alternative venues such as Big and Tall Books, Luna Lounge and Largo. The hosts connect it to Mr. Show and its cast, and praise comics who still perform.

segments.title: Alt comics' style and Mitch Hedberg
segments.summary: The hosts describe alt comedy as observational and less setup-punchline, avoiding racism and homophobia. Mitch Hedberg is discussed and a joke is quoted. Bill Burr's criticism of the alt scene as a comedy womb is recounted.

segments.title: Podcasts and Joe Rogan's influence
segments.summary: Comedy podcasts such as Mark Maron's WTF and the Joe Rogan Experience are discussed. The hosts note Rogan's influence on comedy and the shift of many podcast-launched comics toward right-leaning politics.

segments.title: Social media and podcasts bypassing club gatekeeping
segments.summary: The hosts discuss alt-right podcast comics being booked into clubs based on social media followings, the criticism that some lack stand-up experience, and how social media has changed the gatekeeping of stand-up.

segments.title: One-person shows
segments.summary: Chuck describes the one-person show as plotted, sometimes with pathos, and names Mike Birbiglia, Alex Edelman, Gary Gulman and John Hodgman as examples.

segments.title: Nanette and claptrap
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether Hannah Gadsby's Nanette is comedy, discuss the term claptrap comedy coined by Seth Meyers for applause-driven sets, and note that laughter can be relief.

segments.title: Tig Notaro and the chair bit
segments.summary: Tig Notaro is described as a risk taker, including performing topless after her mastectomy, and her Conan set in which she moved a squeaky chair around the stage for five minutes.

segments.title: Heckling, phones and crowd work
segments.summary: The hosts discuss heckler takedowns going viral, phones in the audience, and crowd work as a major part of some younger comics' acts, with Big Jay Oakerson and Rory Scoville as examples of improvisational crowd work.

segments.title: Working comics and Anthony Jeselnik
segments.summary: The hosts praise Kyle Kinane, Anthony Jeselnik (including his book club promoting short books and a Punchline anecdote), and Mulaney's Manhattan run. Rory Scoville is also mentioned.

segments.title: Psychology of comedians
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a study of stand-up comedians' higher rates of depression and anxiety, the OLIFE traits (unusual experiences, cognitive disorganization, introverted anhedonia, impulsive nonconformity), and Dave Attell as an example.

segments.title: Comedian lifespan study
segments.summary: A 2016 Australian study found stand-up comedians died about 10 years earlier than the general population, and died younger than comic and dramatic actors. Most died of natural causes, but more died of non-natural causes.

segments.title: How to start doing stand-up
segments.summary: The hosts advise writing at least five minutes of material, practicing it, performing at low-stakes open mics, not reading from notes, and structuring a set with a strong opener, risky middle, and strong closer or callback.

segments.title: Should comedy topics be off limits?
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether any topics should be off limits for stand-up. They discuss offense, punching up versus punching down, Sarah Silverman's controversial material, Ronny Chang's punching up, and Dave Chappelle's recent style. Josh offers an explanation for the rise of right-leaning comedians.

segments.title: Listener mail: Paper Ghosts shout-out
segments.summary: A listener writes that the novel Paper Ghosts by Sarah Addison Allen mentions the show in chapter 18, where a character queues an episode on chaos theory.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and invite stories of encountering the show in the wild.
